title: Filling and polishing a chipped marble or stone top
subtitle: Repair a chip in a marble, granite, or limestone surface using tinted two-part epoxy stone adhesive, ground flush and polished to match
excerpt: How to repair a chip in a marble or natural stone surface. Covers cleaning the chip, mixing and tinting epoxy stone adhesive, filling and curing, grinding back with diamond pads, and polishing to match the surrounding surface.
sourceNotes: UK stone trade and conservation repair practice (open access). Natural stone restoration guidance from British Stone (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: A two-part clear or white epoxy adhesive formulated for use on marble, granite, and other natural stone. It sets hard and can be tinted with dry pigment powders to match the stone colour. Available in different viscosities: liquid for hairline cracks, gel or paste for chip filling.

A flexible resin pad with synthetic diamond particles of a defined grit size, used to grind and polish stone surfaces. Pads are used in sequence from coarse (50-200 grit for levelling) through to very fine (1500-3000 grit for polishing). Used dry or wet; wet produces a finer finish and reduces dust.

content.text: A chip in marble or granite breaks both the visual surface and the protective polish seal. The repair fills the chip with tinted
. BEGINNER: the main skill is colour-matching; the work itself is methodical.

Clean the inside of the chip with acetone or isopropyl alcohol on a cotton bud to remove all dust, grease, and cleaning product residue. The epoxy will not bond to a greasy surface. Allow the stone to dry fully before applying the adhesive.

Mix a tiny trial amount of epoxy and stir in dry pigment powders (ochre, umber, white, black) until the colour matches the stone when pressed flat against it. The colour shifts slightly as the epoxy sets and when polished: test a match on a spare piece of stone or card before filling the chip.

Mix the tinted epoxy according to the instructions. Apply with the filling knife, pressing firmly into the chip and overfilling slightly above the stone surface. Lay a small square of cling film over the fill and press flat to reduce air bubbles and minimise the amount of cured epoxy to grind back. Allow to cure fully, typically two to four hours at room temperature.

Remove the cling film. The cured epoxy will be slightly proud of the stone surface. Work through the diamond polishing pad sequence from 200 grit to 400, 800, 1500, and 3000 grit, used wet, flattening the fill progressively and restoring the polish level. A handheld orbital sander or random orbital polisher speeds this up considerably on large chips.

attrs.symptom: Fill colour does not match the surrounding stone after polishing
attrs.cause: The epoxy colour was assessed before polishing; polishing changes the apparent colour of both the fill and the stone.
attrs.fix: Apply a thin coat of clear stone sealer over the fill and surrounding area while wet to simulate the polished state, and adjust pigment quantities in a new test batch.

attrs.symptom: Fill pulls out of the chip cleanly after curing
attrs.cause: The chip surfaces were contaminated with grease or moisture before filling.
attrs.fix: Clean the chip again with acetone, dry thoroughly, and re-fill.
